result.markdown: --- title: "GiBleed — Exercises" subtitle: "Find your own significant association in a larger, boolean-only cohort" format: html: df-print: kable execute: eval: false --- Download the worksheet (.R) Source (.Rmd) View solutions # How to use this sheet You did the whole workflow in the [GiBleed tutorial](gibleed.html). Now find a **different** association yourself. Fill the `____` blanks, run each chunk, and read the output. Remember: GiBleed has **no numeric values**, so every clinical variable is a **boolean** flag (`format = "binary"`) and age is anchored to **2019**. Worked, executed [solutions](gibleed_solution.html) are one click away. ## Setup (run this first) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DSI); library(DSOpal); library(dsBaseClient); library(dsOMOPClient) builder <- DSI::newDSLoginBuilder() builder$append(server = "nairobi", url = "https://nairobi.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "douala", url = "https://douala.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") builder$append(server = "dakar", url = "https://dakar.datashield.live", user = "ethiopia", password = "P@ssw0rd", profile = "omop") conns <- DSI::datashield.login(logins = builder$build()) ds.omop.connect(resource = "omop_demo.gibleed", symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ``` ::: --- # Exercise 1 — Explore the medications The tutorial looked at *conditions*. Now explore **drugs**: which are most common, and how many patients take **celecoxib** (an anti-inflammatory / NSAID)? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # STEP 1 — pooled prevalence of the top drugs (by distinct patients) ds.omop.concept.prevalence("____", metric = "persons", top_n = 12, scope = "pooled", symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled # STEP 2 — confirm celecoxib's concept_id and how many patients take it ds.omop.concept.lookup(1118084, symbol = "omop", conns = conns)$pooled ``` ::: **Question:** Roughly how many patients are on celecoxib? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Drugs live in the **`drug_exposure`** table. Celecoxib is `concept_id = 1118084`. ::: # Exercise 2 — Build a boolean table Build a wide table `M` with **sex**, **age** (anchored to 2019), a boolean **GI-bleed** flag (`192671`) and a boolean **celecoxib** flag (`1118084`). Ratify it, and read each flag's prevalence. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = ____), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 192671, format = "____", name = "gi_bleed"), omop_variable(table = "drug_exposure", concept_id = 1118084, format = "____", name = "celecoxib") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide")) recipe_execute(rec, out = c(study = "M"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) ds.colnames("M", datasources = conns); ds.dim("M", datasources = conns) as.data.frame(ds.table("M$celecoxib", datasources = conns)$output.list[["TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts"]]) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint `year = 2019`; both clinical flags are `format = "binary"` (a yes/no presence). ::: # Exercise 3 — Is celecoxib associated with GI bleeding? Fit a logistic regression of GI bleed on age, sex and celecoxib. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- ds.glm(formula = "M$gi_bleed ~ M$age + M$sex + M$____", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) fit$coefficients ``` ::: **Question:** Is celecoxib a significant predictor (p < 0.05)? In which direction (OR above or below 1)? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint The third predictor is `M$celecoxib`. Expect a **significant** odds ratio **above 1** (an NSAID raising GI-bleed odds). Age and sex should be non-significant in this older cohort. ::: # Exercise 4 — A different outcome: does age predict a fracture? Unlike GI bleed, some outcomes *do* rise with age. Build a table with sex, age, and a boolean **forearm-fracture** flag (`concept_id = 4278672`), then model it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_fx <- omop_recipe( variables = list( omop_variable(table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id", format = "sex_mf", name = "sex"), omop_variable_age(name = "age", year = 2019), omop_variable(table = "condition_occurrence", concept_id = 4278672, format = "binary", name = "fx_forearm") ), output = omop_output(name = "study", type = "wide")) recipe_execute(rec_fx, out = c(study = "FX"), symbol = "omop", conns = conns) fit_fx <- ds.glm(formula = "FX$fx_forearm ~ FX$____ + FX$____", family = "binomial", datasources = conns) fit_fx$coefficients ``` ::: **Question:** Which predictor is significant now? How does that contrast with the GI-bleed model? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Hint Predictors are `FX$age` and `FX$sex`. Here **age** should be significant — older patients fall more — whereas in the GI-bleed model the *comorbidity*, not age, carried the signal. ::: # Open challenge Pick any condition or drug from the tutorial's prevalence chart, add it as a boolean flag, and test whether it predicts GI bleed. **First check its prevalence** (Section 7 of the tutorial showed what happens to a near-100% or near-0% outcome). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # YOUR CODE HERE ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} DSI::datashield.logout(conns) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} A larger cohort means more power — but also remember the per-patient disclosure gate still runs on every result, and a degenerate (all-yes / all-no) outcome still can't be modelled. :::
